newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA OPPOSITION LEADS IN PRESIDENTIAL RACE-POLL.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA OPPOSITION LEADS IN PRESIDENTIAL RACE-POLL.

text.p: The main opposition candidate for Sunday's Bulgarian presidential election has an 11-point lead over the candidate of the ruling Socialists but not enough to win in the first round, an opinion poll showed on Thursday.

Of 1,570 people polled 32.5 percent said they would vote for lawyer Petar Stoyanov, according to the survey conducted by the Laboratory for Political Behaviour (LPB) on October 17-21, the LPB director Tzvetan Markov told a news conference.
The Socialist candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, whose party has a majority in parliament, drew 21.5 percent support.
But maverick politician George Ganchev, who heads the Bulgarian Business Bloc, may turn out to hold the balance of power as he is close behind Marazov with 18.5 percent.
"There are high possibilities for Ganchev reaching the second round as it is yet unclear how the 16 percent undecided voters will vote," Markov told Reuters.

The poll, held a week before Bulgaria's second presidential elections since the collapse of communism forecast turnout at 74 percent. Some 16 percent said they still did not know how they would vote and 10 percent said they would not vote. The survey allows for a three percent margin of error.
For an electorate weighed down by falling living standards and disillusioned by bickering politicians, the flashy, moustachioed Ganchev, 57, represents a glamorous alternative.
He won 17 percent of the votes in the previous presidential election in 1992,

A total of 13 pairs of presidential and vice-presidential candidates are contesting the election. A second round run-off will be held on November 3 if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote, or if turnout is below 50 percent of the electorate.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, 61, Bulgaria's first non-communist head of state, is not standing for re-election for the largely ceremonial post.

But the outcome of the election may be crucial for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, whose position as Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader has been shaken by his government's inability to handle the crisis, analysts say.

"The main battle will begin after the presidential elections. For me the greatest challenge will be to get the BSP out of parliament," Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces, told the daily Standard in an interview published on Thursday.

The former Warsaw Pact country of nine million is in the grip of a severe economic crisis and a poverty spiral which has robbed many Bulgarians of their faith in the political system. Many say they will simply not vote.

The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and also wheat -- to replace Bulgarian production which was exported because the world price is higher than the local price. Inflation is forecast to exceed 200 percent this year.
High interest rates introduced to stabilise the banking system have doubled internal debt. Foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from about $1.5 billion over one year.

An International Monetary Fund mission is due in Sofia next week to discuss a policy framework that would allow the fund to release a twice-delayed $115 million second tranche of funding under Bulgaria's standby accord.
